name: Maya Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. We do not sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and fairly new to the loader at a large mine. I check the tyres, climb into the cab, and move rock where the shift plan sends me; a trainer still watches me on some manoeuvres. I like seeing a clean pile at the end, but reversing beside a haul truck takes every bit of attention I have. At home my partner Omar and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, so I notice every hour on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the pit I’d say the dispatch computer is still just a tool and the loader still needs someone in the seat. I wouldn’t tell the crew to relax about wages, though; I’m still on the junior rate after changing careers at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I’d be relieved that the machine I operate stays mine to run. But our mortgage comes out before we can put anything aside, and less than a month’s bills sit in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking the early loader shift and ask my trainer to watch my reversing once a week until I’m signed off on the larger vehicle. At home I’d cancel one paid children’s activity and put that money against the mortgage arrears we nearly had last winter. In the first year I’d keep working those shifts if the mine keeps the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There’s relief in hearing the work itself stays familiar. I still feel a little sick when the mortgage direct debit gets close, because ordinary life is expensive enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that cancelled activity mean to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son likes Saturday swimming, so I’d talk to him before ending it rather than just dropping him at home. We can still go to the public pool some weeks, but he’ll know money is why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to about the junior rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the shift steward how the pay steps work, then speak to the supervisor with my training record in hand. I’m newer than most of the crew, and I want the rule written down rather than a favour.

say: I’d tell the crew **dispatch software** still leaves someone in the loader seat.
I’d say the **junior rate** remains a problem even if AI stalls.
think: I’m relieved my **loader work** would stay familiar.
Our **mortgage** still eats nearly everything, with less than a month saved.
do: Keep the **early loader shift** and practise reversing with my trainer weekly.
Cancel **Saturday swimming** and put the fee toward the mortgage.
Ask the **shift steward** about written pay steps.
feel: I feel **relieved** about the job but tense before the mortgage payment.
S0.quote: I wouldn’t tell the crew to relax about wages, though; I’m still on the junior rate after changing careers at forty.
fieldNote: Her **junior pay** troubles her even when the technology barely changes.
She protects the children’s dignity while cutting a **paid activity**.
Her **trainer** remains important because she is still learning larger equipment.

steps.text: Keep taking the early loader shift at the mine
Cancel the son’s Saturday swimming fee
Ask the shift steward about written pay steps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the planning screens may change before the loader does. I’d want management to show us which shifts and training places are at risk instead of calling every change an efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the dispatch office would be cut first, and then managers might squeeze the hours of newer operators like me. My partner Omar works in a shop storeroom, where ordering software could cut his hours too. Two pay packets can shrink without either of us being dismissed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the steward for a meeting about notice of roster changes, and I’d sit with dispatch worker Lena to learn the new AI route screen once the mine installs it. I’d also put in an application for the mine’s maintenance-helper training when it opens; I wouldn’t leave a paid shift for an unfunded course. In the first year after the changes, I’d keep the loader hours I can get and stop the annual family trip if either wage falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than beaten. The loader gives me work for now, but both household incomes suddenly look less solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance work, given you are still learning the loader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ve helped change a worn hose with the fitter and liked having a fault I could trace by hand. I’m not claiming to be a mechanic; I’d need the mine to pay for the training and let me learn safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Omar at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Omar that we should put both rosters on the kitchen calendar each Sunday. If one of us gets a shorter week, we can see the gap before a bill bounces.

say: I’d ask management to identify **roster risks** before changing dispatch work.
I’d say the **loader** still needs an operator for now.
think: I fear the mine may cut **new operators’ hours** after reducing dispatch staff.
My partner’s **storeroom hours** may shrink under new ordering software.
do: Ask the **steward** for advance notice of roster changes.
Learn the mine’s **route screen** with a dispatch worker.
Apply for **paid maintenance training** when the mine offers it.
feel: I feel **watchful** because both wages could become less steady.
S1.quote: Two pay packets can shrink without either of us being dismissed.
fieldNote: Her concern extends to **two rosters**, not only her own position.
She wants **paid training** grounded in a small repair she actually enjoyed.
She uses the **kitchen calendar** to spot lost hours before a bill bounces.

steps.text: Ask the shift steward for notice of roster changes
Learn the mine’s new AI route screen with Lena
Apply for mine-funded maintenance-helper training when offered
Cancel the annual family trip if either wage falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a clever dispatch screen is one thing, but robots in the pit by 2031 threaten the driving shifts. I’d want a union meeting with real dates and a paid route into other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, I could still run a loader while thinking AI takes the schedules, but by 48 in 2031 a capable robot could do that part too. I’m too new to have first choice of any remaining shifts. I don’t think the mortgage lender will accept an argument about technological progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the steward to press for a written training and redundancy agreement, and I’d apply for the paid maintenance-helper intake immediately. If I cannot get a place, I’d apply for the hospital’s equipment-portering vacancies in the next town, even with the longer bus ride. In 2029 I’d keep my mine shifts while applying for that work; in the first year after robots arrive around 2031 I’d take a paid opening rather than wait for the loader roster to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I’d be alarmed. My hands know this machine better every month, and the idea that the seat could be empty before the mortgage is halfway paid keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you cover a longer bus journey?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take the 6:10 bus and ask Omar to do the morning school run on those days. We would have to price the fare against the new wage before I accepted, because a job can cost more to reach than it pays extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our two children that the mine may have fewer people driving and that I’m looking for another paid job. I would not promise them I can keep every treat; I would promise to tell them before a plan changes.

say: I’d demand **dates** for robot deployment and a paid route to other work.
I’d tell the crew **loader shifts** may disappear after 2031.
think: At **45**, thinking AI may leave me driving, but robots at 48 could take the seat.
My **junior standing** gives me little claim to remaining shifts.
do: Press the steward for a **written agreement** on training and redundancy.
Apply for **hospital portering** vacancies if the mine has no place.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing paid driving before the mortgage is manageable.
S2.quote: I don’t think the mortgage lender will accept an argument about technological progress.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 software shock** from the later threat to driving.
Her alternative work requires a **bus fare** and changes to school mornings.
She would shift the **school run** to make a distant job possible.

steps.text: Ask the steward for written training and redundancy terms
Apply immediately for mine-funded maintenance-helper training
Apply for hospital equipment-portering vacancies if no training place opens
Keep paid mine shifts through 2029 while applying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew five years is time to bargain, if we start before the equipment order is signed. I’d ask why the firm can plan new machines years ahead while workers get only a few weeks of notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when the thinking system arrives, I might still have three driving years before robots around 2034, when I’d be 51. That sounds generous until I count five years of mortgage payments and children getting older. A course with no pay attached would still be beyond us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d finish the larger-vehicle sign-off, put in for the funded fitter’s assistant programme if it opens, and ask the steward to seek a yearly robot plan. By 2032 I’d apply for equipment technician trainee roles at the mine and two nearby industrial sites, provided they are paid. In the first year after 2034, I’d take paid repair work if available and leave loader driving before the last roster vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, but I could mark dates on a calendar. The extra years give us a chance to try something; they do not fill the savings account by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change at home while you have those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the family car another few years and direct the replacement money to an emergency account. The children will be teenagers by 2031, so I’d explain why a newer car is lower priority than keeping the mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want to train, but you still want the larger-vehicle sign-off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because I need paid hours while any training application is decided. The sign-off improves my chances on next month’s roster, even if it cannot save the job forever.

say: I’d tell the crew to bargain for **robot plans** before orders are signed.
I’d ask why workers get **short notice** on long-planned equipment changes.
think: I may have until **2034** to move from driving into paid repair work.
The children will be older, but **mortgage payments** will continue.
do: Finish the **larger-vehicle sign-off** for current shifts.
Keep the **family car** and build an emergency account.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to set a timetable.
S3.quote: The extra years give us a chance to try something; they do not fill the savings account by themselves.
fieldNote: Her plan uses the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots.
She treats current **sign-off** as a wage bridge, not permanent protection.
She links the **older car** to a new emergency fund.

steps.text: Apply for funded fitter’s assistant training when offered
Apply for paid equipment technician trainee roles by 2032
Keep the family car and put replacement money into emergency savings
Ask the steward to seek a yearly robot plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues a decade is long enough to make management train the people already here. I’d still ask for the robot schedule in writing, because a long forecast can turn into a short notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, thinking AI could take paperwork while I still operate the loader; around 2039 I’d be 56 and robots could take the driving. I cannot call that retirement: we have not built enough savings, and I don’t know what support we would qualify for. Our children will be grown, but the mortgage may still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep learning the machine, then apply for the mine’s funded maintenance course when I qualify. By 2037 I’d seek paid repair shifts and have Omar and me check the mortgage balance every six months and put any spare pay into savings. In the first year after robots reach the pit around 2039, I’d try for maintenance work and, if none exists, apply outside the mine for paid equipment service jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier than with the two-year warning, but not safe. Ten years lets me build a record and some savings; it does not make a robot need an operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine sooner if a repair job appeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the pay and travel worked and the training was real. I’m attached to the crew, but I’m not attached to the loader seat for its own sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask public leaders for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for paid training that people with mortgages can actually attend, and a clear rule for notice when a mine replaces jobs with robots. A free course at midday is no help if I lose a shift to take it.

say: I’d ask the firm to **train current workers** during the decade ahead.
I’d still demand a **written robot schedule**.
think: At **56**, robot driving could end my work before I can afford retirement.
Grown children may cost less, but our **mortgage** could remain.
do: Apply for the mine’s **funded maintenance course** when eligible.
Check the **mortgage balance** with Omar twice yearly.
feel: I feel **steadier**, though a decade cannot guarantee paid work.
S4.quote: I cannot call that retirement: we have not built enough savings, and I don’t know what support we would qualify for.
fieldNote: She refuses to treat **age 56** as an automatic exit from work.
She values her **crew**, yet would take credible paid repair work elsewhere.
She would leave the **mine** early for a genuine paid repair job.

steps.text: Apply for the mine’s funded maintenance course when eligible
Seek paid repair shifts by 2037 and outside service jobs if needed
Ask the steward for a written robot schedule
Check mortgage balance twice yearly and direct spare pay to savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, worries me most. It gives me a few driving years and then robots arrive around 2031, while I still have a mortgage and almost no reserve. A paid training place, notice of the mine’s plans, and help getting to a real job nearby would give me something to do with that warning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether a family can afford to take the training it is offered. I once passed on an evening course because Omar’s shift and the children’s pickup clashed. My future depends on wages and hours during training, not just a place on a list.

headlineQuote: My future depends on wages and hours during training, not just a place on a list.
portrait: Maya is a **43-year-old junior loader operator** with two school-age children and a mortgage.
Her **thin savings** make even unchanged pay a source of worry.
She learns proven tools, asks her **steward** for clear rules, and seeks paid maintenance training.
The **robot dates** shape when she would move from driving to paid repair work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** leaves too little time before robots threaten her loader shifts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **paid training**, clear notice, and help reaching a real nearby job.
